Each night every page is re-chunked and inserted with a new ID (random UUID or counter). Unchanged pages therefore add exact duplicates (the paragraph appears three times after three runs), edited pages add a new version while the old chunks stay (stale content), and deleted pages are never removed (answers quoting removed policies). Index growth of a few percent a night comes from edits plus any chunks whose boundaries shift when text near the start of a document changes, which can alter every following chunk.

Each night the pages the job treats as changed (edited, or merely re-dated) are re-chunked and inserted under new IDs (random UUID, counter or version-stamped key) without removing the previous chunks. Every edit therefore adds a full new copy of that page while the old copy stays: a paragraph that survived three edits exists three times (duplicates), superseded wording stays retrievable (stale content), and deleted pages are never removed (answers quoting removed policies). A few percent growth per night fits this only if a small share of pages is rewritten per night; if the job re-inserted every unchanged page too, the index would roughly double each night, so check growth against the number of changed pages. Boundary shifts make it worse: an edit near the start of a document can move every following fixed-size chunk boundary, so even untouched text gets new chunk hashes and is re-inserted.
